pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, The Water Cycle — the Sun evaporates surface water into invisible vapour, which rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as precipitation, repeating endlessly.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y4 States of matter — 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature'; builds on Y1 Seasonal changes.
• Standards — US (NGSS): approached via grade-3 Earth's Systems (3-ESS2-1 typical seasonal weather) and matter/states; the full interacting-systems water cycle is formalised at Grade 5 (5-ESS2-1) and MS-ESS2-4 (sun + gravity drive the cycling of water). State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach as a continuous, Sun-driven loop with THREE named stages (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) but anchor the WHY (energy) not just the sequence; use discrepant-event demos (drying puddle; cold-can condensation with food-colouring to prove water didn't leak through) to confront the 'water disappears' and 'sweating' misconceptions; stress conservation — the same water changes form and place but is never lost.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name the three stages and state the Sun drives it; Tier B — explain evaporation/condensation as reversible state changes and rate rising with temperature; Tier C — trace runoff, transpiration and groundwater as part of one conserved global system.
bestPractices: Frame the cycle as a continuous loop with no beginning or end and no water lost — counter the memorised 'E-C-P' sequence by asking WHY each step happens (energy in, energy out)

Use discrepant-event demos: a drying puddle (water goes UP as invisible vapour, not into the ground) and condensation on a cold can with food-colouring added to the ice water (droplets are clear, so water did NOT seep through the wall)
Make invisibility explicit — water vapour is a clear gas you cannot see; steam and clouds are already-condensed liquid droplets, not the vapour itself
Have children draw-then-revise their own water-cycle diagram as formative assessment, then add missing arrows (evaporation from land/plants, not just oceans)
Connect rate to temperature with a fair test (warm vs cool water evaporating), aligning to the DfE Y4 objective
keyRepresentations: Closed-loop cycle diagram with labelled arrows (evaporate up, condense, precipitate down, flow back)
A single tracked water droplet/molecule journeying around the loop to make conservation concrete
Sun-as-engine icon driving the whole loop
Cross-section of land + sea + sky showing all evaporation sources, not a single ocean arrow
commonMisconceptions: 'The water disappears / soaks away' when a puddle dries — actually it becomes invisible water vapour in the air
'Condensation seeped through the cup' (the sweating model) — the water condensed FROM the air onto the cold surface
Clouds and steam ARE water vapour — actually both are visible LIQUID droplets; vapour is invisible
Water rises straight up into a waiting cloud, or a cloud scoops water and drops it elsewhere — vapour moves in all directions and clouds form by condensation
The cycle is only evaporation + condensation (omitting precipitation, runoff, groundwater, transpiration)

learn.summary: For learners aged 7–9, teach the water cycle as a continuous, Sun-driven loop in which the same water repeatedly changes form and place but is never lost. Anchor the WHY (energy in from the Sun, energy out as vapour cools) rather than only memorising the evaporation→condensation→precipitation sequence. Use discrepant-event demonstrations to confront the 'water disappears' and 'condensation seeped through the cup' misconceptions, and make the invisibility of water vapour explicit (clouds and the visible white 'steam' or mist above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets or ice crystals, not the vapour itself).

activities.title: Sun-driven water-cycle model the learner controls
feedback: If the learner says the vapour 'disappears', show that in the follow-one-droplet view the tagged droplet is still there, just rendered faint — hidden as a clear gas, not gone.
If the learner says clouds ARE the vapour, point out the vapour is faint/near-invisible while the cloud is made of visible tiny water droplets (or ice crystals) that formed when the vapour cooled.
If the learner expects rain to be the end, run the droplet round again so they see it flow back and re-evaporate: the loop has no end.
If the learner thinks the water moves by itself, have them turn the Sun control down and notice the whole engine slow — the Sun is the driver.
activities.rationale: The target concept is a driven, conserved loop; letting the child act on the drive (the Sun control) and track one conserved droplet makes energy-drive, conservation and endlessness concrete rather than a memorised word order. A live heat control and the faint-vapour-then-visible-cloud rendering are intended to target the 'clouds are vapour' and 'water disappears' misconceptions named in the source misconception research. The controllable heat dial, faint-to-visible vapour rendering and droplet-tagging are illustrative mechanisms, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
learnerActions: Over a land-and-sea scene, raise a Sun/heat control and watch puddles and sea surfaces give off vapour that rises, cools into clouds, and falls as rain that flows back to the sea.
Turn the Sun control down and observe the whole loop slow: evaporation slows, fewer clouds form, and rain becomes less — stating in your own words why.

Switch to a 'follow one droplet' view: tag a single glowing droplet and watch it evaporate, become near-invisible vapour, condense inside a cloud, fall as rain, and flow back to the start again — never disappearing.

Watch a drying puddle on a hard surface and describe out loud where the water goes (UP into the air as invisible vapour), rather than saying it just vanished. (On soil, some puddle water also soaks into the ground.)
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle is an endless loop driven by the Sun's energy, and the same water is conserved — it only changes form (liquid↔invisible vapour) and place, never being used up or destroyed.

activities.title: Drying puddle and cold-can discrepant-event investigation
feedback: If the learner predicts the water is destroyed or 'used up', revisit with a covered dish: droplets usually appear on the underside of the lid when it is cooler than the water — hidden, not gone.
If the learner thinks the can's droplets came from inside, point to their clear colour versus the coloured water inside: coloured water cannot pass through and arrive clear.

When interpreting the result, note that droplets form readily on the cold surface in typical humid indoor air but fewer may appear in very dry air, so judge by what you actually observe rather than expecting a guaranteed outcome.
Reinforce that clouds and the white 'steam' (mist) you can see above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets (clouds may also hold ice crystals); the vapour itself is a clear gas you cannot see.
activities.rationale: Discrepant events that contradict the learner's prediction are used to surface and challenge the specific, documented misconceptions (water disappears; condensation seeped through the cup). The food-colouring test gives a clear, checkable outcome that the condensed water came from the air.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
DfE Y4 States of matter: pupils should 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature'.
learnerActions: Before observing a puddle (or a shallow dish of water) left in a warm, sunny spot, predict and write down what will happen to the water and WHY.

Watch over time as it dries, then explain where the water went — into the air as invisible vapour. (Water in a dish cannot soak away, so it can only have gone into the air; a puddle on soil or grass can also lose some water by soaking into the ground.)
Add a few drops of food colouring to ice water in a can or cup, then watch for droplets forming on the OUTSIDE of the cold surface and check their colour.
Explain why any outside droplets are CLEAR, not coloured: the water condensed from the air onto the cold surface — it did not leak through the wall.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaporated water becomes invisible vapour in the air (it doesn't vanish), and 'sweating' on a cold surface is water condensing FROM the surrounding air, not water seeping through the container.

activities.title: Fair test: does temperature change how fast water evaporates?
feedback: If the learner changes more than one thing (amount of water, dish size, surface area, air flow or location), remind them a fair test keeps everything the same except the one variable being tested — here, temperature.
If the learner compares a sunny with a shaded dish and calls it a temperature test, point out that sunlight differs too; to test temperature alone, warm the water while matching the lighting.
Connect the result back to the whole cycle: more heat speeds evaporation, just as the Sun's warmth does on a hot day.
activities.rationale: A controlled comparison that isolates temperature (warm vs cool water under matched conditions) aligns with the DfE Y4 objective and gives the learner evidence that heat increases evaporation rate; a separate sun-vs-shade comparison surfaces the Sun as the energy source without being mislabelled a temperature-only test. The sun-vs-shade observation inspects the puddle on the ground, not the Sun itself.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 States of matter: pupils should 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature'.
learnerActions: Fill two similar open dishes with the same amount of water — one with warm water and one with cool water — keeping dish size, surface area, air flow and location the same so that only the water temperature differs.
Predict which will lose water faster and why.

Check them over time (e.g. mark or measure the water level) and compare which lost water faster, remembering that the warm water slowly cools towards room temperature, so the difference may be small and is clearest early on.
State your conclusion from what you observed: if the warmer dish lost more water, this supports the idea that higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.

As a separate question about the Sun's role, compare a puddle in the sun with one in the shade (observing the puddles on the ground) and discuss which dries faster and why — remembering the puddles may also differ in size and depth.
activities.intendedInsight: Under matched conditions, warmer water evaporates faster, so the rate of evaporation rises with temperature. In everyday life a hot day speeds drying, and on a sunny day both the warmth and the direct sunlight raise the rate — the Sun's heat is what warms water and drives the cycle.

activities.title: Draw, revise and trace your own water-cycle diagram
feedback: If the diagram only shows an ocean arrow, prompt: where else does water evaporate from? (wet land, puddles, plants).
If the diagram is a one-way line ending at rain, ask how the fallen rain gets back up — close the loop.
If the Sun is missing, ask what provides the energy to lift the water as vapour.
Talking a droplet through 'where do you go next, and are you ever destroyed?' can surface conservation; keep it anchored to the real causes (heat drives it, cooling condenses it).
activities.rationale: Draw-then-revise works as formative assessment that exposes the learner's current model (often omitting precipitation, land/plant evaporation or the Sun), and constructing the labelled loop builds the conservation and endlessness intuition that recall alone does not. The droplet-narration is an optional way to voice conservation, not the primary causal explanation.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
learnerActions: Draw your own diagram of the water cycle from memory, labelling arrows for where water goes.
Compare it with a closed-loop cross-section showing land, sea and sky, then add any missing arrows — especially evaporation from land and plants, not just the ocean.
Draw the loop so it has no beginning and no end, and mark the Sun as the engine that drives it.
Optionally extend by adding runoff, groundwater and transpiration from plants as parts of one conserved system.
Explain to a partner, or to an imagined water droplet, where the water goes next and whether it is ever destroyed.
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle is one continuous, conserved system — water evaporates from many sources (sea, land, plants), condenses, precipitates and flows back, driven by the Sun, with none lost.

constraints: Teach three named stages (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) but anchor WHY each happens (energy in from the Sun, energy out as vapour cools); do not let the learning reduce to memorising the E-C-P word order.

Make invisibility explicit: water vapour is a clear gas you cannot see; clouds and the visible white 'steam' (mist) above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets or ice crystals, not the vapour itself.
Stress conservation: the same water changes form and place but is never lost, used up or destroyed.

A static labelled loop with tap-to-reveal names can teach vocabulary but cannot show the Sun-driven motion or conservation on its own; use it as a vocabulary scaffold alongside an activity that shows the loop moving and closing.

Recall-only sequencing or multiple-choice items (e.g. ordering evaporation→condensation→precipitation, or picking the Sun's role) can assess naming but do not by themselves build the loop/conservation intuition; use them to check vocabulary, not as the main teaching.
A richly rendered 3D landscape adds scenery but the cycle is conceptually a planar cross-section; extra depth is optional and not required for the causal insight.

Any evaporation-rate fair test must isolate temperature (match surface area, water amount, air flow and lighting); a sunny-vs-shaded comparison tests the Sun's role, not temperature alone, because sunlight differs between the two.
Shade/sun comparisons should observe the puddle or ground (or the drying water), never ask a child to look at or through a cover toward the Sun.

Tier expectations: naming the three stages and that the Sun drives it (introductory); explaining evaporation/condensation as reversible state changes with rate rising with temperature (intermediate); tracing runoff, transpiration and groundwater as one conserved global system (advanced).
Correct the 'vapour rises straight up into a waiting cloud / a cloud scoops and drops water elsewhere' picture: vapour moves in all directions and clouds form by condensation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (the DfE Y4 statement and the Beyond Penguins misconceptions page); the NGSS 3-ESS2-1 citation is marked verified but concerns seasonal weather representation rather than the water cycle directly, so it was not used to support water-cycle teaching claims.

The source notes the full interacting-systems water cycle is typically formalised later (around Grade 5 / middle school in NGSS); for ages 7–9 keep groundwater/transpiration as optional extension, consistent with the advanced tier.
No comparative efficacy or necessity claims are asserted for any medium; the interactive model, discrepant events, diagram and narration are complementary options with stated affordances and limits.

The food-colouring condensation demo assumes typical humid indoor air so droplets form on the cold surface; outcomes depend on actual humidity and temperature and should be presented as observed, not guaranteed.

The evaporation fair test isolates temperature (warm vs cool water under matched conditions); sun-vs-shade is kept as a separate question about the Sun's role because sunlight confounds a temperature-only test, and the everyday 'hot day' framing in the intendedInsight distinguishes warmth from direct sunlight.
The 'understanding consolidates around age nine' statement is from an unverified source and is reported as a claim, not established fact.

assess.poeTask: Put a little water in a clear sealed jar or zip-bag and stand it in a sunny window. Before observing, ask the child to PREDICT what happens to the water level and whether water appears on the lid, and to say WHY. The stated reason — the water evaporates and re-condenses and none can escape the sealed container — is the diagnostic part; a child who predicts the level simply drops with nothing on the lid still holds the 'water is used up' idea.
probeDeeper: Why does the puddle vanish faster on a hot sunny day than a cold cloudy one?
If you sealed the puddle under a clear plastic dome, where would the water end up, and why?
Does the same water fall as rain more than once, or is every raindrop brand new?
What would happen to the whole cycle if the Sun switched off?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun's heat turned the puddle water into invisible water vapour (evaporation); it rose, cooled and condensed into cloud droplets; when the droplets grow heavy they fall back as rain (precipitation). The water isn't used up — it moves round a never-ending, Sun-driven loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The water just dried up and it's gone' — treats the puddle disappearing as the water being destroyed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Catch the vapour: a covered dish shows the water reappears as droplets — hidden, not gone.
errorPatterns.distractor: The heat destroys the water and it disappears for good.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot say where the water went; no link to later rain

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Clouds are made of smoke/steam/cotton, not the puddle's water' — severs cloud from the evaporated water
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link breath-on-cold-glass condensation to cloud droplets forming from the risen vapour.
errorPatterns.distractor: Rain comes from clouds, but clouds aren't made from the puddle's water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes clouds as unrelated stuff, can't close the loop to rain

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Rain falls and stops there' — runs the cycle as a one-way line, not a loop
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace one water molecule round the loop repeatedly until the cycle closes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Water goes down as rain and stops there; it doesn't go back up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot connect fallen rain back up to evaporation

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Water moves round by itself' — omits the Sun as the energy that drives the cycle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare drying rates of a shaded vs a sunny puddle to surface the Sun's role.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: never mentions the Sun/heat as the driver

responseLevels.gap: Says the water 'dried up and is gone'; cannot connect the puddle to later rain.
responseLevels.full: Explains the Sun heats water to vapour, which cools and condenses into cloud, falls as precipitation and evaporates again — a closed, Sun-driven loop with water conserved — and transfers this to a covered-dish or different-climate case.
responseLevels.partial: Names evaporation, condensation and precipitation as separate steps but cannot say the Sun drives them or that the same water is conserved and recirculated.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A puddle in the playground disappears on a sunny day. Where did the water go, and how could it end up falling as rain again later?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the water 'dried up and is gone' cannot connect the vanished puddle to future rain; only a child holding the conserved, Sun-driven cycle links the disappearance to rain returning.
